messages.body_plain:
Right -- a vector (or usually an array) beta must be
either data or parameter, not a mixture of both.

What Jiaqiang suggests will work if you don't need
beta as a multivariate parameter anywhere, such as
the mean of a multivariate normal or Dirichlet parameter.

For instance, if you need a vector parameter
mu as the mean of a normal, you'd use:

data {
    double mu_1;  // constant for 1
}
parameters {
    double mu[M-1]; // array of params 2:M
}
derived parameters {
    vector(M) mu_vec;  // vector
    mu_vec[1] <- mu_1;
    for (m in 2:M) mu_vec[m] <- mu[m-1];
}

You then get M-1 sampled values correspdonding
to the array mu.

I haven't thought about what we can do if the parameters
need to form a simplex, as for a discrete or multinomial
distro parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: stan::agrad::var for boost math
messages.body_plain:
I finally found the doc I was looking for, which outlines
what you need to do to integrate a new scalar type into
Boost:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/using_udt/concepts.html

We should be good to go, because stan::agrad::var is
defined for all the built-in arithmetic operations and
assignments and because I just defined std::numerics<stan::agrad::var>,
everything else can be derived by template metaprogramming
according to footnotes 1-3 on the above page.

Here's a nice example of bindings for arbitrary
precision real arithmetic:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_48_0/boost/math/bindings/rr.hpp

Given that the default implementations of std::numeric_limits<T>
for non-primitive type T just threw exceptions for all the
constants, I don't think they'll get created willy nilly, because
we haven't seen any such exceptions.

Good templated code will use the std::numeric_limits<T> template
for constants.

There's also a nice example of how to do more general comparison
operations.  I'll retrofit these onto our auto-dif, which should
make them more flexible.  (It's exactly problems like this at
an even more basic level that prohibited our use of the other
auto-dif libs -- all sorts of basic ops were missing or ill-defined
to return constants rather than refs or things like that.)

- Bob

messages.subject: implicit type checks & error messages for multivar normal
messages.subject_clean: implicit type checks & error messages for multivar normal
messages.body_plain:
I'm looking at distributions_multi_normal and had
a bunch of thoughts.

0.  We only need to use our matrix functions if
we don't know what the types are.  Once we know
what the types are for the propto overrides,
we can use the built-ins like .transpose() which
are much faster (e.g., no intermediate memory
and no copying in the case of transpose()).  We'll
know where we need to promote.

1.  We probably want to have a parameterization
in terms of Sigma_inverse.  Inverting the matrix
every time is going to be expensive.
det(inv(Sigma)) = 1/det(Sigma), so that's no problem.

2.  We need more checks on dimensionality.  For instance,
we need y.size() == mu.size() == Sigma.rows() == Sigma.cols().

3.  For the errors, the same char* function doesn't make
sense.  If I understand properly, the value y
will get substituted into function, but that's not right,
as we don't want multi_normal_log<y>(y) to come out.

4.  Some of the checks we can probably drop as they'll raise
the right errors through eigen.  For instance, checking the
covariance matrix is positive definite happens implicitly
as part of determinant anyway.   We probably do want to check
symmetry if that's not implied.

- Bob

messages.subject: Eigen matrix package in R (Doug Bates & Dir Eddelbuettel)
messages.subject_clean: Eigen matrix package in R (Doug Bates & Dir Eddelbuettel)
messages.body_plain:
This was sent to the Eigen mailing list by
Doug Bates and Dirk Eddlbuettel.  I replied
to Dirk's comment on Andrew's blog entry that
we were also using Rcpp thanks to Malecki's
guidance (and help).

I think Doug's planning to rewrite lmer using
Eigen because it's faster and more flexible than
whatever he was using before.  He's been pretty active
on the Eigen list (and I hope he pushes through some
of the proposed changes for symmetric matrices, as
they'll help us in the Stan implementation).

- Bob

-------- Original Message --------
Subject: [eigen] Paper regarding availability of Eigen classes from R
Date: Thu, 1 Dec 2011 12:25:55 -0600
From: Douglas Bates <ba...@stat.wisc.edu>
Reply-To: ei...@lists.tuxfamily.org
To: ei...@lists.tuxfamily.org
CC: Dirk Eddelbuettel <e...@debian.org>

R (www.R-project.org <http://www.R-project.org>) is an interpreted language widely used in
statistical computing and Bioinformatics.  It can be extended with
contributed packages, many of which are made available through CRAN,
the Comprehensive R Archive Network.

Dirk Eddelbuettel, Romain Francois and I have contributed a package
RcppEigen that includes Eigen, release 3.0.3, and some "glue" using
Rcpp classes to allow communication between R and the compiled C++
code.  Dirk and I wrote an introduction, available as
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RcppEigen/RcppEigen.pdf,
introducing the R package and Eigen classes.  In particular we compare
several approaches to obtaining least squares solutions through
decompositions available in Eigen.

We would welcome suggestions regarding the code or the presentation.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] censored [& truncated] data
messages.body_plain:
We definitely don't want people to have to
modify the C++ code to implement censored or
truncated models.  But our models will look
different again from those of BUGS and JAGS.

I don't quite understand their Weibull model,
but here's how it'll work for a normal distro.

First, we can't handle NA values -- all data
must be in the form of an integer or floating point
value.  So if y[1:N] is all the data with some
NA values, let

Outcomes and predictor for uncensored values:

data {
     double C;            // censoring point

     int N_uc;            // number of uncensored items
     double y_uc[1:N_uc]; // measurement of uncensored item
     double x_uc[1:N_uc]; // predictors for uncensored items

     int N_c;             // number of censored items
     double x_c[1:N_c];   // predictors for censored items
}
model {
     for (n in 1:N_uc)
         y_uc[n] ~ normal(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma);

     for (n in 1:N_c)
         1 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_lb(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma, C));
}

First, note that although y_uc[n] must be less than
C, this is not a constraint on the variable in the Stan
sense of wanting to transform it.  So it remains double
rather than double(,C) in the declaration.

The first sampling is not truncated.  This is equivalent
in terms of contribution to log likelihood to:

     0 ~ bernoulli(...);
     y_uc[n] ~ normal_ub(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma, C);

Andrew and Jennifer do a bunch of these calcs in their book.

What's needed in Stan to make this fly:

1.  All the cumulative distributions.  For instance,
c_normal_lb(mu,sigma,L) needs to be included as a special
function and defined to be  Pr[X > L] if X ~ normal(mu,sigma).

You'll of course need the Weibull.  All the necessary
cumulative distributions are in Boost and we'll use the
densities in Stan for their derivatives.  So it's a fair
bit of work per density for all of this.

2.  Allowing general expressions on the LHS of samples (as
in the 1 above).  Very unusual from a BUGS perspective, but
no obstacle for Stan.  I'll fix that right now and post when
I've done it.

If you want, you can also sample latent parameters
y_c, as in:

     for (n in 1:N_c) {
         y_hat <- alpha * x_c[n] + beta;
         1 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_lb(y_hat,sigma,C));
         y_c[n] ~ normal_lb(y_hat,sigma,C);
     }

Then they can play with others.  In this case, it might also
be conceptually clearer (though less computationally efficient)
to have parallel loops:

for (n in 1:N_uc) {
         y_uc[n] ~ normal_ub(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma, C);
         0 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_ub(alpha * x_uc[n] + beta, sigma, C));
}

for (n in 1:N_c) {
         y_c[n] ~ normal_lb(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma, C);
         1 ~ bernoulli(c_normal_lb(alpha * x_c[n] + beta, sigma, C);
}

I'll probably present it this way and then note that the top loop
simplifes to how I wrote it at first, and you can drop the y_c[n]
sampling if you don't need it.

- Bob

On 12/5/11 9:27 AM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> In a BUGS example (vol 1, Mice), we have right censored lifetime
> data (in other words, we only know that the lives of some mice
> would be larger than some points).  For this example, pretending
> we do not have censoring and use stan gm to generate cpp code,
> which would be modified to reflect the censoring, I could have the
> example running.
>
> When computing the log-likelihood, originally we only have
>               lp__ += stan::prob::weibull_log(t[i - 1], r,
> sigma[group[i - 1] - 1]);

messages.subject: function template defaults
messages.body_plain:
Daniel and I came up with a way to merge the
policied and unpolicied function calls using
template defaults.  Daniel then went and pushed
this through the library.  It all worked fine
on our Macs.  Then he tried other compilers and
platforms, which couldn't handle the function
template defaults.

The current standard allows defaults for class
template parameters, but not for function template
parameters.

Eventually, the compilers should catch up to the
new C++11 standard, but I think it'd be nice to run
with the current crop until then.

So I'm suggesting that we switch our functions back
to Boost style for now at least, such as

template <typename T1, typename T2>
inline typename calc<T2,T3>::type
foo(const T1& x1, const T2& x2) {
     return foo(x1,x2,policy<>::type);
}

template <typename T1, typename T2, typename P>
inline typename calc<T1,T2>::type
foo(const T1& x1, const T2& x2, const P& /* ignore */) {
     ... use P() if necessary ...
}

The inline combined with the resolution of the
default policy at compile time and the second function
not paying attention to the actual param means there's
at least no run-time overhead.

The downside is that there's now double the doc
to write, though I think the resulting unpolicied function,
which is what you almost always want to use, will be
clearer to most users.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I committed some code for declaring function
type signatures.  It's in a helper-include file:

src/stan/gm/function_signatures.hpp

It declares the type of all of Stan's built-in
functions.  It doesn't include the basic
binary and unary arithmetic operators, which
are handled in a different branch of the grammar.

As written now, you can't use the arithmetic
operators (i.e., +, -, *, /) for vectors or
matrices.  I could change that later pretty easily.

In order to add a new function to Stan,
a declaration of its type needs to go in the above
file (or the appropriate method called before the
parser is called if you're running programatically).

The function itself needs to be defined for
both doubles and stan::agrad::var inputs in arbitrary
positions.  The simplest way is to fully template
(diff template variable for each argument with a computed
result type).  It's more efficient to override
and define the partial evaluations for the auto-difs
as we do for all the built-ins so far.

When compiling a Stan model file, I check that there's
a unique function.  In the end, I went through and
did the int to double promotion properly.  So if you
declare two functions:

   double foo(int x, double y);
   double foo(double x, int y);

and try to call foo(2,3), you'll get an error, as
both are equally good promotion candidates, requiring
one int to be promoted to a double.  There aren't any functions
that have this kind of pathological signature set in the
built-ins, but who knows what users might do.

Eventually, to make Stan extensible with user-defined
C++ functions, I'll need to have a way to include user
headers and declare the type of new functions.  I'm
thinking something like the following to include a function
foo() mapping a double and vector to a double.

extensions {
     using my::functions; // include in generated code

     include <foo/bar/baz.hpp> // carry over to model includes

     function double f(double,vector); // type info
}

I'm NOT going to do this for the first release, though.
It'll be easy enough to extend the language later in
a backward-compatible fashion.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 12/5/11 8:17 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
 > More generally, we need left censored, right censored, and interval
 > censored:

Exactly.

Right now, you can bound double parameters above, below, or
both and they'll be appropriately transformed (log, log,
logit).  You can also bound double data this way, but that
only comes into the compiled code as an error check.
There are also more complex multivariate bounds for simplexes,
ordered positive values (for ordered logit bounds) and
covariance and correlation matrices.  There are a bunch of
classes in stan::io for this and the unit tests and doc
show how it'll work and provide all the definitions of
the transform, and its log Jacobian determinant.

What we haven't implemented are all the truncated
densities (left, right, both) and all the
cumulative density functions (left, right, both again).
And ideally those'd also get pre-built derivatives.
There's a lot of spade-work left to do building this out
and even more if we want the gradients and proportionality
to be calculated efficiently.

At around 15 distributions total, that'll be
7 variations, each with 2 forms due to error propagation,
for a total of around 210 functions to write.  Each of those
should then get a class to efficiently implement its
gradients.  Makes me tired just thinking about it.

Which ones are the most important for models?  We'll
at least have to do all the ones for the BUGS models.

 > And C might be a vector: different censoring mechanism
 > for each data point.

If there's a different set of lower and upper bound
censoring for each point, we're not going to be able
to declare that as part of the variable definition and
use the simple latent variable method -- we'll have
to evaluate the truncated distributions.

If the bounds are variable, it's even trickier, but
with the cumulatives, it can still be worked out, I think.

Sounds like you'd like to help write the manual!
That's up next.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] censoring w/o cumulative densities
messages.body_plain:
> Which ones are the most important for models?  We'll
> at least have to do all the ones for the BUGS models.

Taking a quick look of bugs examples, Weibull distribution might be the
one used.

I think for the Mice example, I could use the Bernoulli distribution (do the CDF
by myself) to work
around.  It is just easier for me to modify the cpp code (you know I could use if/else, etc.)
instead of reorganizing the data and implementing censoring in stan.
But the later is doable, which means we could leave out the censoring
stuff now if you want.

If Stan supports censoring, the first candidate distributions supported, I think, are
Exponential, Weibull, Log-normal, Gamma.

===
I am a bit confused about declaring uncensored data.  If you declare
censored data as

data {
    double C;
    int N_c;
    double(C, )  y_c[N_c];
}

Are you meaning that if we do not pass data to y_c, stan would
think those are censored (or latent)?  Usually, we can declare the above
constraint for data themselves as well.

On Mon, Dec 5, 2011 at 10:25 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> On 12/5/11 8:17 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> > More generally, we need left censored, right censored, and interval
> > censored:
>
> Exactly.
>
> Right now, you can bound double parameters above, below, or
> both and they'll be appropriately transformed (log, log,
> logit).  You can also bound double data this way, but that
> only comes into the compiled code as an error check.
> There are also more complex multivariate bounds for simplexes,
> ordered positive values (for ordered logit bounds) and
> covariance and correlation matrices.  There are a bunch of
> classes in stan::io for this and the unit tests and doc
> show how it'll work and provide all the definitions of
> the transform, and its log Jacobian determinant.
>
> What we haven't implemented are all the truncated
> densities (left, right, both) and all the
> cumulative density functions (left, right, both again).
> And ideally those'd also get pre-built derivatives.
> There's a lot of spade-work left to do building this out
> and even more if we want the gradients and proportionality
> to be calculated efficiently.
>
> At around 15 distributions total, that'll be
> 7 variations, each with 2 forms due to error propagation,
> for a total of around 210 functions to write.  Each of those
> should then get a class to efficiently implement its
> gradients.  Makes me tired just thinking about it.
>
> Which ones are the most important for models?  We'll
> at least have to do all the ones for the BUGS models.
>
>
> > And C might be a vector: different censoring mechanism
> > for each data point.
>
> If there's a different set of lower and upper bound
> censoring for each point, we're not going to be able
> to declare that as part of the variable definition and
> use the simple latent variable method -- we'll have
> to evaluate the truncated distributions.
>
> If the bounds are variable, it's even trickier, but
> with the cumulatives, it can still be worked out, I think.
>
> Sounds like you'd like to help write the manual!
> That's up next.
>
> - Bob
>

Even if it's easier for you to monkey with the
C++, it won't be easier for our users.

We only need to re-organize the data because
we got it organized for BUGS.  With our own
data, it shouldn't be such a big deal.

I'm afraid there's really no way with the compiled
architecture to do censoring more directly.  Maybe
someone could figure out how to add mixed vectors,
but everything's pretty strongly typed.  I could
add more generic wrappers and override for that, but
it'd be very heavy at run time.

I'll also have to add something to bring lp into
the variable space so it can be hacked directly once
I start doing full type checking.

- Bob

>     Which ones are the most important for models?  We'll

>
>
> Taking a quick look of bugs examples, Weibull distribution might be the

> by myself) to work
> around.  It is just easier for me to modify the cpp code (you know I
> could use if/else, etc.)
> instead of reorganizing the data and implementing censoring in stan.
> But the later is doable, which means we could leave out the censoring
> stuff now if you want.
>
> If Stan supports censoring, the first candidate distributions supported,
> I think, are
> Exponential, Weibull, Log-normal, Gamma.
>
>
> ===
> I am a bit confused about declaring uncensored data.  If you declare
> censored data as
>
> data {
>      double C;
>      int N_c;
>      double(C, )  y_c[N_c];
> }
>
> Are you meaning that if we do not pass data to y_c, stan would
> think those are censored (or latent)?  Usually, we can declare the above
> constraint for data themselves as well.
>
>
>
>
> On Mon, Dec 5, 2011 at 10:25 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com
> <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>     On 12/5/11 8:17 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
>      > More generally, we need left censored, right censored, and interval
>      > censored:
>
>     Exactly.
>
>     Right now, you can bound double parameters above, below, or
>     both and they'll be appropriately transformed (log, log,
>     logit).  You can also bound double data this way, but that
>     only comes into the compiled code as an error check.
>     There are also more complex multivariate bounds for simplexes,
>     ordered positive values (for ordered logit bounds) and
>     covariance and correlation matrices.  There are a bunch of
>     classes in stan::io for this and the unit tests and doc
>     show how it'll work and provide all the definitions of
>     the transform, and its log Jacobian determinant.
>
>     What we haven't implemented are all the truncated
>     densities (left, right, both) and all the
>     cumulative density functions (left, right, both again).
>     And ideally those'd also get pre-built derivatives.
>     There's a lot of spade-work left to do building this out
>     and even more if we want the gradients and proportionality
>     to be calculated efficiently.
>
>     At around 15 distributions total, that'll be
>     7 variations, each with 2 forms due to error propagation,
>     for a total of around 210 functions to write.  Each of those
>     should then get a class to efficiently implement its
>     gradients.  Makes me tired just thinking about it.
>
>     Which ones are the most important for models?  We'll
>     at least have to do all the ones for the BUGS models.
>
>
>      > And C might be a vector: different censoring mechanism
>      > for each data point.
>
>     If there's a different set of lower and upper bound
>     censoring for each point, we're not going to be able
>     to declare that as part of the variable definition and
>     use the simple latent variable method -- we'll have
>     to evaluate the truncated distributions.
>
>     If the bounds are variable, it's even trickier, but
>     with the cumulatives, it can still be worked out, I think.
>
>     Sounds like you'd like to help write the manual!
>     That's up next.
>
>     - Bob

messages.body_plain:
I broke the parser again.  The currently checked
in version will appear to parse, but won't generate
indexes for arrays, as in a[n] will get generated
just as a.

At this point, it's probably best if everyone
waits for me to fix this before trying to build
more models.

The last bug was a clause ordering issue in
the expressions.  But all these things interact
in the top-down parser in ways I can't quite
get to the bottom of.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] censoring w/o cumulative densities
messages.body_plain:
For now, I have changed the mice example using
1 ~ bernoulli(....).  It is running now.

On Tue, Dec 6, 2011 at 12:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Thanks -- I'll work on:
>
> > Exponential, Weibull, Log-normal, Gamma.
>
> Even if it's easier for you to monkey with the
> C++, it won't be easier for our users.
>
> We only need to re-organize the data because
> we got it organized for BUGS.  With our own
> data, it shouldn't be such a big deal.
>
> I'm afraid there's really no way with the compiled
> architecture to do censoring more directly.  Maybe
> someone could figure out how to add mixed vectors,
> but everything's pretty strongly typed.  I could
> add more generic wrappers and override for that, but
> it'd be very heavy at run time.
>
> I'll also have to add something to bring lp into
> the variable space so it can be hacked directly once
> I start doing full type checking.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> On 12/6/11 11:52 AM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> >    Which ones are the most important for models?  We'll
> >    at least have to do all the ones for the BUGS models.
> >
> >
> > Taking a quick look of bugs examples, Weibull distribution might be the
> > one used.
> >
> > I think for the Mice example, I could use the Bernoulli distribution (do
> > the CDF
> > by myself) to work
> > around.  It is just easier for me to modify the cpp code (you know I
> > could use if/else, etc.)
> > instead of reorganizing the data and implementing censoring in stan.
> > But the later is doable, which means we could leave out the censoring
> > stuff now if you want.
> >
> > If Stan supports censoring, the first candidate distributions supported,
> > I think, are
> > Exponential, Weibull, Log-normal, Gamma.
> >
> >
> > ===
> > I am a bit confused about declaring uncensored data.  If you declare
> > censored data as
> >
> > data {
> >     double C;
> >     int N_c;
> >     double(C, )  y_c[N_c];
> > }
> >
> > Are you meaning that if we do not pass data to y_c, stan would
> > think those are censored (or latent)?  Usually, we can declare the above
> > constraint for data themselves as well.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Mon, Dec 5, 2011 at 10:25 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com
> > <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
> >
> >    On 12/5/11 8:17 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> >     > More generally, we need left censored, right censored, and interval
> >     > censored:
> >
> >    Exactly.
> >
> >    Right now, you can bound double parameters above, below, or
> >    both and they'll be appropriately transformed (log, log,
> >    logit).  You can also bound double data this way, but that
> >    only comes into the compiled code as an error check.
> >    There are also more complex multivariate bounds for simplexes,
> >    ordered positive values (for ordered logit bounds) and
> >    covariance and correlation matrices.  There are a bunch of
> >    classes in stan::io for this and the unit tests and doc
> >    show how it'll work and provide all the definitions of
> >    the transform, and its log Jacobian determinant.
> >
> >    What we haven't implemented are all the truncated
> >    densities (left, right, both) and all the
> >    cumulative density functions (left, right, both again).
> >    And ideally those'd also get pre-built derivatives.
> >    There's a lot of spade-work left to do building this out
> >    and even more if we want the gradients and proportionality
> >    to be calculated efficiently.
> >
> >    At around 15 distributions total, that'll be
> >    7 variations, each with 2 forms due to error propagation,
> >    for a total of around 210 functions to write.  Each of those
> >    should then get a class to efficiently implement its
> >    gradients.  Makes me tired just thinking about it.
> >
> >    Which ones are the most important for models?  We'll
> >    at least have to do all the ones for the BUGS models.
> >
> >
> >     > And C might be a vector: different censoring mechanism
> >     > for each data point.
> >
> >    If there's a different set of lower and upper bound
> >    censoring for each point, we're not going to be able
> >    to declare that as part of the variable definition and
> >    use the simple latent variable method -- we'll have
> >    to evaluate the truncated distributions.
> >
> >    If the bounds are variable, it's even trickier, but
> >    with the cumulatives, it can still be worked out, I think.
> >
> >    Sounds like you'd like to help write the manual!
> >    That's up next.
> >
> >    - Bob
> >
> >

messages.body_snippet:
Grab some coffee before reading this one.

I've been thinking a bit about what we can do
about the emerging problem Daniel's running into

messages.subject: passing policies
messages.body_plain:
I've been thinking more about error policies.

One thing we can do is treat them as statically
configured in Boost and require resetting a global
default rather than allowing our functions to
be configurable one-by-one.

On the other hand, if they're configurable one-by-one
and I can add variable names in the graphical models
to the policies, that'd be awesome for debugging
complex models.

If we do allow declared policies, we'll need to
pass them through to all the embedded functions.
If we just assume a single master config, we won't need
to bother with this.

- Bob

> On Thu, Dec 8, 2011 at 12:53 PM, Jiqiang Guo<guo...@gmail.com>  wrote:

This is exciting -- we're printing reasonable
messages for errors already.

Given that the only normal in the model is

   beta ~ normal(0, 10);

and the beta isn't declared to be transformed, the beta
parameter had to come in as a NaN value.  I don't see how
this could come about -- the only thing that happens to it
is adding momentum amounts and the gradient of normal_log(0,10)
shouldn't be too sharp.

Is it repeatable, Daniel?  It always goes to NaN
in the second step?

One issue is whether we then want to just catch
these exceptions in the sampler loop, report
them, then try again (up to some limit so we
don't go into an infinite loop).

I'm not sure what JAGS does, but I've often seen
pages and pages of error messages about NaN values
found in evaluations (usually in gamma functions).

- Bob

On Thu, Dec 8, 2011 at 12:19 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Grab some coffee before reading this one.
>
> I've been thinking a bit about what we can do
> about the emerging problem Daniel's running into
> adding the following to our densities:
>
>   1.  error handling  (default/user policy)
>   2.  proportionality (no/[var/constant per arg])
>   3.  truncation      (lb/no, ub/no)
>
> We know now how to use template metaprogramming to
> reduce the choice of variable/constant per arg
> for proportional calcs to a single function using
> an is_var<T>::Yes templated class constant.
>
> But now we have the same problem for the combo of
> the other choices, especially the error policies,
> which I suggested be factored into two forms, with
> and without an error policy until all the compilers
> catch up with template function defaults.
>
> For instance, the road we're going down now has:
>
>    normal_log(y,mu,sigma);
>    normal_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lb_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
>    normal_lb_log(",error_policy);
>
>    normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
>    normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
>    normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);
>
>    normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma);
>    normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lb_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
>    normal_lb_propto_log(",error_policy);
>
>    normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
>    normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
>    normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);
>
> Given that we have around 20 densities, that's around
> 320 functions to write, document, and test.  Gulp.
>
> Maybe I've been reading too much Boost code and
> too many template books, but how about a mega-template
> solution.  This is the kind of thing that general
> policy types were meant to deal with.
>
> We could have a single heavily templated function,
> with a declaration like:
>
> template <typename T_outcome,
>          typename T_loc,
>          typename T_scale,
>          typename T_lb,
>          typename T_ub,
>          bool Prop_to,
>          typename Policy>
>
> inline calculated_return<T_outcome,T_loc,T_scale,T_lb,T_ub>::type
>
> normal_log(T_outcome y,
>           T_loc mu,
>           T_scale sigma,
>
>           T_lb lb = stan::nil,
>           T_ub ub = stan::nil,
>
>           Policy p = default_policy<>::policy);
>
> The same way we can use is_var<T_scale>::Yes to statically
> compute if a variable is a parameter or a constant, we
> can also define a templated class constant has_value<T_lb>::Yes
> that will statically eval to true if T_lb has a value other
> than a special dummy type stan::nil.  We'd have to actually
> complicate the calculated return a bit to coerce T_lb, but
> that's doable:
>
> calcuated_return<...,promotion_type<T_lb>::type,...>
>
> which would evaluate to double if T_lb == nil.
>
> I think we can drop the non-policy version, which would leave us
> with a single function per density.
>
> Now in the definition of normal_log(), we'll need some
> heinous branching, which I wouldn't otherwise condone,
> to wit:
>
> normal_log(...) {
>  // error checking goes here; e.g., if sigma < 0,
>
>  calculated_result<...>::type lp(0);
>
>  if (!Prop_to)
>    lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI;
>
>  if (!Prop_to || is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
>    lp -= log(sigma);
>
>  if (!Prop_to
>      || is_var<T_out>::Yes
>      || is_var<T_loc>::Yes
>      || is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
>    lp -= 0.5 * square((y - mu)/sigma);
>
>  if ( (is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes || is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes)
>       && (!Prop_to || is_var<T_lb>::Yes || is_var<T_ub>::Yes
>                    || is_var<T_loc>::Yes || is_var<T_scale>::Yes) {
>      if (is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes)
>          lp -= log(normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,ub,pol)
>                    - normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
>      else if (!is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes))
>          lp -= log(1.0 - normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
>      else if (...)
>          lp -= ...;
>      else
>          lp -= ...;
>  }
>
>  return lp;
> }
>
>
> As before, all the conditionals will be defined statically.
>
> The question is whether this is easier than writing 16 functions,
> each of which looks like one path through this tangle of if-thens.
>
> Also, having to set lp(0) is annoying, as it'll add another
> auto-dif variable to the stack that's really useless.
>
> We can combine the first two statements, to get
>
>  calculated_result<...>::type
>  lp(Prop_to : 0.0 : NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI);
>
> but given that we're usually in the Prop_to case, this
> isn't going to be much help in practice.
>
> We could solve the problem with template expressions, but
> I think that's going too far.
>
> Another alternative would be to pass in an lp value to
> increment.  That works for our use case, at least, but it
> adds a very complex calculated argument to the argument
> list (I'd think it should go first), as in:
>
> normal_log(calculated_result<...>::type lp,
>           T_outcome y,
>           T_loc mu,
>           T_scale sigma,
>
>           T_lb lb = stan::nil,
>           T_ub ub = stan::nil,
>
>           Policy p = default_policy<>::policy);
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: bounds checking, part two
messages.body_plain:
On 12/8/11 4:08 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
 >  > dpois(1, lambda = 0)
 > [1] 0
 >  > dpois(0, lambda = 0)
 > [1] 1
 >  > dpois(2, lambda = 0)
 > [1] 0
 >  > dpois(-2, lambda = 0)
 > [1] 0

That makes sense mathematically if you
think of Poisson(N|lambda) being defined over
all integers for all N no matter what lambda is.
I think Boost has the same kind of behavior.

Also, we're following Mssrs. Gelman, Carlin, Stern,
and Rubin, the appendix of whose book states
that Poisson(N|lambda) is defined for lambda > 0 (strictly)
and N = 0, 1, 2, ...

The problem is that even if lambda is a parameter
which we bound > 0, we can get 0 due to underflow
when we do the exp(x) reverse transform for
x < -400 or so.

We also need gradients.  The problem is
that poisson_log(N,lambda) doesn't have a gradient
if N is negative, or if lambda is not greater than
zero.

We also want to be more helpful in flagging client
errors.  If they put in count data with negative
counts, we want to trap it as early as possible as
an error.

Another issue for us is that we want to be able
to

Like Boost, R handles the RHS differently.

 > dpois(-2,-2)
[1] NaN
Warning message:
In dpois(x, lambda, log) : NaNs produced

Unlike Boost, R would make Matt happy, because it
treats the location and sampled value symmetrically.
Boost complains if you do y ~ norm(mu,sigma) with
anything but a finite mu, though it'll allow infinite y.
(That makes sense given their design because they
construct an object for norm(mu,sigma) and catch the
error at construction time if you've used illegal
parameters.)

 > So it might be better that when lambda=0,
 > poisson_log(N, lambda) gives log(0) when N is not 0.
 > I am not sure about this since even I am not sure about
 > log(0) is legitimate.

log(0) produces -infinity in IEEE arithmetic.
We'd like to make sure our distribution code handles
the infinities well, too.  For instance, R also does
sensible things with all the infinity cases for the normal:

 > dnorm(1/0,0,1)
[1] 0
 >
 > dnorm(1/0,0,1,log=T)
[1] -Inf
 > dnorm(0,1/0,1)
[1] 0
 > dnorm(0,1/0,1,log=T)
[1] -Inf
 > dnorm(0,0,1/0)
[1] 0
 > dnorm(0,0,0/1)
[1] Inf

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Poisson bounds checking
messages.body_plain:
On 12/8/11 4:52 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
 > I think at the end of that, we've decided that:
 > lambda == 0 (regardless of N) is a domain error?
 > or is it
 > lamdba == 0 when N>  0 is a domain error?

Here's my thinking:

log_poisson(n,lambda)

   = log Poisson(n|lambda) if +infinity > lambda > 0 and n >= 0

   = domain error if lambda < 0 or n < 0

   = domain error if n is NaN or lambda is NaN

The NaN error and other errors may just lead to
NaN propagation with the right traits set.

That leaves a few boundary conditions undecided.

   = domain error    if lambda = +infinity

If it were zero, the partial derivative w.r.t. lambda is
-infinity, and when we do +infinity + -infinity, we'll
get a NaN.  So I think it's safe to leave this
an error.

   = 0   if n = 0, lambda = 0

Just branching and returning 0 makes the gradient 0,
too.  It could also throw an error.

   = domain error  if n > 0, lambda = 0

This could return -infinity if the gradient
makes sense:

lim(L -> 0) d/d.lambda log Poisson(n|lambda)

I didn't work through whether this limit makes
sense or blows up.  The gradient would probably
have to be plumbed in by hand.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] templates to tame density code bloat?
messages.body_plain:
All I can say is . . . wow!  I'm glad we have a whole team on this, and now I can see why development on Bugs stalled at some point.

On Dec 8, 2011, at 12:19 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Grab some coffee before reading this one.
>
> I've been thinking a bit about what we can do
> about the emerging problem Daniel's running into
> adding the following to our densities:
>
>   1.  error handling  (default/user policy)
>   2.  proportionality (no/[var/constant per arg])
>   3.  truncation      (lb/no, ub/no)
>
> We know now how to use template metaprogramming to
> reduce the choice of variable/constant per arg
> for proportional calcs to a single function using
> an is_var<T>::Yes templated class constant.
>
> But now we have the same problem for the combo of
> the other choices, especially the error policies,
> which I suggested be factored into two forms, with
> and without an error policy until all the compilers
> catch up with template function defaults.
>
> For instance, the road we're going down now has:
>
>    normal_log(y,mu,sigma);
>    normal_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lb_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
>    normal_lb_log(",error_policy);
>
>    normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
>    normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
>    normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);
>
>    normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma);
>    normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lb_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
>    normal_lb_propto_log(",error_policy);
>
>    normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
>    normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);
>
>    normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
>    normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);
>
> Given that we have around 20 densities, that's around
> 320 functions to write, document, and test.  Gulp.
>
> Maybe I've been reading too much Boost code and
> too many template books, but how about a mega-template
> solution.  This is the kind of thing that general
> policy types were meant to deal with.
>
> We could have a single heavily templated function,
> with a declaration like:
>
> template <typename T_outcome,
>          typename T_loc,
>          typename T_scale,
>          typename T_lb,
>          typename T_ub,
>          bool Prop_to,
>          typename Policy>
>
> inline calculated_return<T_outcome,T_loc,T_scale,T_lb,T_ub>::type
>
> normal_log(T_outcome y,
>           T_loc mu,
>           T_scale sigma,
>
>           T_lb lb = stan::nil,
>           T_ub ub = stan::nil,
>
>           Policy p = default_policy<>::policy);
>
> The same way we can use is_var<T_scale>::Yes to statically
> compute if a variable is a parameter or a constant, we
> can also define a templated class constant has_value<T_lb>::Yes
> that will statically eval to true if T_lb has a value other
> than a special dummy type stan::nil.  We'd have to actually
> complicate the calculated return a bit to coerce T_lb, but
> that's doable:
>
> calcuated_return<...,promotion_type<T_lb>::type,...>
>
> which would evaluate to double if T_lb == nil.
>
> I think we can drop the non-policy version, which would leave us
> with a single function per density.
>
> Now in the definition of normal_log(), we'll need some
> heinous branching, which I wouldn't otherwise condone,
> to wit:
>
> normal_log(...) {
>  // error checking goes here; e.g., if sigma < 0,
>
>  calculated_result<...>::type lp(0);
>
>  if (!Prop_to)
>    lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI;
>
>  if (!Prop_to || is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
>    lp -= log(sigma);
>
>  if (!Prop_to
>      || is_var<T_out>::Yes
>      || is_var<T_loc>::Yes
>      || is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
>    lp -= 0.5 * square((y - mu)/sigma);
>
>  if ( (is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes || is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes)
>       && (!Prop_to || is_var<T_lb>::Yes || is_var<T_ub>::Yes
>                    || is_var<T_loc>::Yes || is_var<T_scale>::Yes) {
>      if (is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes)
>          lp -= log(normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,ub,pol)
>                    - normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
>      else if (!is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes))
>          lp -= log(1.0 - normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
>      else if (...)
>          lp -= ...;
>      else
>          lp -= ...;
>  }
>
>  return lp;
> }
>
>
> As before, all the conditionals will be defined statically.
>
> The question is whether this is easier than writing 16 functions,
> each of which looks like one path through this tangle of if-thens.
>
> Also, having to set lp(0) is annoying, as it'll add another
> auto-dif variable to the stack that's really useless.
>
> We can combine the first two statements, to get
>
>  calculated_result<...>::type
>  lp(Prop_to : 0.0 : NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI);
>
> but given that we're usually in the Prop_to case, this
> isn't going to be much help in practice.
>
> We could solve the problem with template expressions, but
> I think that's going too far.
>
> Another alternative would be to pass in an lp value to
> increment.  That works for our use case, at least, but it
> adds a very complex calculated argument to the argument
> list (I'd think it should go first), as in:
>
> normal_log(calculated_result<...>::type lp,
>           T_outcome y,
>           T_loc mu,
>           T_scale sigma,
>
>           T_lb lb = stan::nil,
>           T_ub ub = stan::nil,
>
>           Policy p = default_policy<>::policy);
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] templates to tame density code bloat?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] templates to tame density code bloat?
messages.body_plain:
After rereading the original email and Bob's comment on issue 14, I'm convinced we should template it out as suggested.

I'll finish out the Weibull distribution broken out so we can continue to build out more models, then I'll work on refactoring the distributions.

On Dec 8, 2011 9:32 PM, "Andrew Gelman" <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> All I can say is . . . wow!  I'm glad we have a whole team on this, and now I can see why development on Bugs stalled at some point.
>
> On Dec 8, 2011, at 12:19 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > Grab some coffee before reading this one.
> >
> > I've been thinking a bit about what we can do
> > about the emerging problem Daniel's running into
> > adding the following to our densities:
> >
> >   1.  error handling  (default/user policy)
> >   2.  proportionality (no/[var/constant per arg])
> >   3.  truncation      (lb/no, ub/no)
> >
> > We know now how to use template metaprogramming to
> > reduce the choice of variable/constant per arg
> > for proportional calcs to a single function using
> > an is_var<T>::Yes templated class constant.
> >
> > But now we have the same problem for the combo of
> > the other choices, especially the error policies,
> > which I suggested be factored into two forms, with
> > and without an error policy until all the compilers
> > catch up with template function defaults.
> >
> > For instance, the road we're going down now has:
> >
> >    normal_log(y,mu,sigma);
> >    normal_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);
> >
> >    normal_lb_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
> >    normal_lb_log(",error_policy);
> >
> >    normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
> >    normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);
> >
> >    normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
> >    normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);
> >
> >    normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma);
> >    normal_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,error_policy);
> >
> >    normal_lb_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
> >    normal_lb_propto_log(",error_policy);
> >
> >    normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U);
> >    normal_ub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,U,error_policy);
> >
> >    normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U);
> >    normal_lub_propto_log(y,mu,sigma,L,U,error_policy);
> >
> > Given that we have around 20 densities, that's around
> > 320 functions to write, document, and test.  Gulp.
> >
> > Maybe I've been reading too much Boost code and
> > too many template books, but how about a mega-template
> > solution.  This is the kind of thing that general
> > policy types were meant to deal with.
> >
> > We could have a single heavily templated function,
> > with a declaration like:
> >
> > template <typename T_outcome,
> >          typename T_loc,
> >          typename T_scale,
> >          typename T_lb,
> >          typename T_ub,
> >          bool Prop_to,
> >          typename Policy>
> >
> > inline calculated_return<T_outcome,T_loc,T_scale,T_lb,T_ub>::type
> >
> > normal_log(T_outcome y,
> >           T_loc mu,
> >           T_scale sigma,
> >
> >           T_lb lb = stan::nil,
> >           T_ub ub = stan::nil,
> >
> >           Policy p = default_policy<>::policy);
> >
> > The same way we can use is_var<T_scale>::Yes to statically
> > compute if a variable is a parameter or a constant, we
> > can also define a templated class constant has_value<T_lb>::Yes
> > that will statically eval to true if T_lb has a value other
> > than a special dummy type stan::nil.  We'd have to actually
> > complicate the calculated return a bit to coerce T_lb, but
> > that's doable:
> >
> > calcuated_return<...,promotion_type<T_lb>::type,...>
> >
> > which would evaluate to double if T_lb == nil.
> >
> > I think we can drop the non-policy version, which would leave us
> > with a single function per density.
> >
> > Now in the definition of normal_log(), we'll need some
> > heinous branching, which I wouldn't otherwise condone,
> > to wit:
> >
> > normal_log(...) {
> >  // error checking goes here; e.g., if sigma < 0,
> >
> >  calculated_result<...>::type lp(0);
> >
> >  if (!Prop_to)
> >    lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI;
> >
> >  if (!Prop_to || is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
> >    lp -= log(sigma);
> >
> >  if (!Prop_to
> >      || is_var<T_out>::Yes
> >      || is_var<T_loc>::Yes
> >      || is_var<T_scale>::Yes)
> >    lp -= 0.5 * square((y - mu)/sigma);
> >
> >  if ( (is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes || is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes)
> >       && (!Prop_to || is_var<T_lb>::Yes || is_var<T_ub>::Yes
> >                    || is_var<T_loc>::Yes || is_var<T_scale>::Yes) {
> >      if (is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes)
> >          lp -= log(normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,ub,pol)
> >                    - normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
> >      else if (!is_non_nil<T_ub>::Yes && is_non_nil<T_lb>::Yes))
> >          lp -= log(1.0 - normal_cumulative(mu,sigma,lb,pol));
> >      else if (...)
> >          lp -= ...;
> >      else
> >          lp -= ...;
> >  }
> >
> >  return lp;
> > }
> >
> >
> > As before, all the conditionals will be defined statically.
> >
> > The question is whether this is easier than writing 16 functions,
> > each of which looks like one path through this tangle of if-thens.
> >
> > Also, having to set lp(0) is annoying, as it'll add another
> > auto-dif variable to the stack that's really useless.
> >
> > We can combine the first two statements, to get
> >
> >  calculated_result<...>::type
> >  lp(Prop_to : 0.0 : NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI);
> >
> > but given that we're usually in the Prop_to case, this
> > isn't going to be much help in practice.
> >
> > We could solve the problem with template expressions, but
> > I think that's going too far.
> >
> > Another alternative would be to pass in an lp value to
> > increment.  That works for our use case, at least, but it
> > adds a very complex calculated argument to the argument

I just did a mondo commit, including all the type
inference.

I'm now checking all the models in the BUGS folders.

I had to change a few models that used multivariates.  These
need to have the appropriate vector or matrix types.

I also put a model good_all.stan in the test folder
that shows how the code gets generated for lvalues
and expressions.  The trick is that matrices in Eigen
need (m,n) notation, whereas everything else is [m][n].

to make some substantial changes to things like
the grammar to deal with operator precedence and
push the type checking through.

Other than the R interface, this is about it for
the baseline Stan 1.0.  There's still optimization
and all the truncated distributions, but that doesn't
all need to go out in 1.0.

messages.subject: release planning
messages.body_plain:
No way we can release Stan 1.0 (beta?) before
January.  It should be pretty stable as of yesterday
in terms of what's already done.

My list of what remains to do is:

1.  user manual
2.  error handling / arithmetic robustness
3.  discrete sampling
4.  Rstan (calls, convergence, ESS)
5.  make JAGS Rats model faster
6.  30 or so more BUGS models
7.  paper

I'm pretty sure Daniel and I can knock out 1 and 2
in a week or two.

We need to talk more about 3.

4 should be reasonably easy, especially with help from
Malecki.  Most of the connections are in place, but we
also need to test cross-platform.

I don't know what to do about 5 given.  Maybe Andrew
will relent when we show a bunch of models for
which Stan is faster.

The risk with 6 is that the models will expose
problems with everything else.

Maybe we can punt on 7 until after the release.

Daniel tried to get precompiled headers working without
any luck -- if you (Matt) can help out, that'd be great.

- Bob

messages.subject: Jacobians and lp__ += vs. ~
messages.body_plain:
On 12/11/11 1:15 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
 > I have some doubts about this.  It looks to me
 > the LHS is directly plugged into the "log-posterior",
 > which is not correct to me.  Where is the Jacobian?

Thanks!  You're absolutely right -- my suggestion
was totally buggy.

It's only safe to transform the left-hand-side of a
twiddle (sample) operator if it's all data.  That's
the equivalent of BUGS's odd combo:

    x <- ...
    x ~ ...

JAGS makes you do data transforms in a separate block,
and that's also possible, but not required, in Stan.

Jiaqiang's correction made me realize that we can encode
the Jacobians directly with no problem in Stan.

> we could can specify prior on
> derived parameters.

> parameters {

>    double(0,) sigma;
> }
>
> derived parameters {
>    double(0,) tau;
>    tau<- 1 / square(sigma);
> }
>
> model {
>    tau ~ gamma(.001, .001);
> }

The way to think about Stan is that:

     a ~ foo(b,c);

is just a convenient way to write

     lp__ = lp__ + foo_log(a,b,c);

where lp__ is the running total log probability
and foo_log is the log probability function for Foo.

(Now that we have type checking, I need to add
in "lp__" as a known variable before this'll work --
I'll post a note when I do that later.)

So your example just reduces to:

    pow(sigma,-2) ~ gamma(1E-3,1E-3);

And as you point out, we're still missing the Jacobian.

You can add that back in by:

    pow(sigma,-2) ~ gamma(1E-3,1E-3);
    lp__ = lp__ + log(abs(-2 * pow(sigma,-3));

Stan will also let you write the whole model this
way and not use any ~ at all, replacing the above with:

    lp__ = lp__ + gamma_log(pow(sigma,-2), 1E-3, 1E-3);
    lp__ = lp__ + log(abs(-2 * pow(sigma,-3));

This is making me think I should implement the +=
operator, at least.

In general, if we transform, we also need the log
absolute derivative added in:

    g(y) ~ foo(...);
    lp__ = lp__ + log(abs(g'(y))

where g'(y) is the derivative of the transform.

If y is multivariate, you need the whole log absolute
determinant of the Jacobian:

     log(abs(determinant(Jacobian(g)))

Automating this all with auto-dif would require second
order auto-dif, because we still need to differentiate
the final lp__ w.r.t. the parameters.

Maybe for Stan 2.0.  It's the same second order extension
we'll need to do Hessians via auto-dif.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Damn -- that's too bad.

We can use default arguments to functions, right?
I hope it's only a problem with pre C++11 compilers if
that default determines a template parameter.  If
not, then I'm with you -- I'd rather not have to write
four base functions (+/- truncated above, +/- truncated below)
per density.

I'd rather not lean on compiler features that aren't
well supported yet.  It'll do things like break
the interface from R in default installations and make
installing Stan a real pain.

So I think it'd be better to just have two functions:

    foo_log(....) {
        return foo(....,static_default_policy);
    }

    foo_log(...,policy) {
        ... real work here based on policy ...
    }

That's what Boost does, so there's probably not a better
portable way to do it.

We could just implement the second and I could generate
code in Stan to include the default policies.  But that
doesn't seem ideal if others might want to use our C++
API (which I don't think is out of the question given our
ability to do auto-dif).

My plate's pretty clear right now, so I can dive in and
help with these.  Are you (Daniel) going to be around
tomorrow (Monday)?  If so, I'd like to work on a single
class to get it in the right shape.  After that, I think
the others should be pretty easy.

I'll try to read up a bit on Boost's metaprogramming as I'm
guessing they have all the stuff we'll need in place already.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] templates to tame density code bloat?
messages.body_plain:
Default arguments to functions: no. Not without C++11 compilers. For example:

1) No default argument works:
template <typename Policy>
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& ) {
   return;
}
...
testFunction (boost::math::policies::policy<>());

2) Default template argument works with C++11 compiler
template <typename Policy = boost::math::policies::policy<> >
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& ) {
   return;
}
...
testFunction (boost::math::policies::policy<>() );
// DOES NOT WORK: testFunction ();

3) Default template argument and function argument works with C++11 compiler:
template <typename Policy = boost::math::policies::policy<> >
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& = Policy() ) {
   return;
}
...
testFunction (); // THIS WORKS!
testFunction (boost::math::policies::policy<>() );

4) Does not work(even with C++11):
template <typename Policy >
inline void
testFunction (const Policy& = boost::math::policies::policy<>() ) {
   return;
}
...
testFunction ();   // Does not work.

I'll do some research to see if it's not well supported. We know that
it works with clang++ and g++ 4 in windows with an appropriate flag.
Wei had trouble with clang from Xcode 4, but maybe it was compiling
fine and it was a problem with the parser at that point?

messages.body_plain:
The limit

  lim(lambda -> 0) d/d.lambda log_Poisson(n|lambda)

is +infinity, but it is properly defined. I think it is correct to set

  log_Possion(n, lambda) = -infinity if n>0 and lambda=0

Wei

On Thu, Dec 8, 2011 at 6:08 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> On 12/8/11 4:52 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > I think at the end of that, we've decided that:
> > lambda == 0 (regardless of N) is a domain error?
> > or is it
> > lamdba == 0 when N>  0 is a domain error?
>
> Here's my thinking:
>
> log_poisson(n,lambda)
>
>  = log Poisson(n|lambda) if +infinity > lambda > 0 and n >= 0
>
>  = domain error if lambda < 0 or n < 0
>
>  = domain error if n is NaN or lambda is NaN
>
> The NaN error and other errors may just lead to
> NaN propagation with the right traits set.
>
> That leaves a few boundary conditions undecided.
>
>  = domain error    if lambda = +infinity
>
> If it were zero, the partial derivative w.r.t. lambda is
> -infinity, and when we do +infinity + -infinity, we'll
> get a NaN.  So I think it's safe to leave this
> an error.
>
>  = 0   if n = 0, lambda = 0
>
> Just branching and returning 0 makes the gradient 0,
> too.  It could also throw an error.
>
>  = domain error  if n > 0, lambda = 0
>
> This could return -infinity if the gradient
> makes sense:
>
> lim(L -> 0) d/d.lambda log Poisson(n|lambda)
>
> I didn't work through whether this limit makes
> sense or blows up.  The gradient would probably
> have to be plumbed in by hand.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Poisson bounds checking
messages.body_plain:
The limit values that the Poisson log-pdf actually gives in those last
few scenarios are
lambda=0, n=0: logp=0, grad_lambda=–1 (because 0log0 is basically 0)
lambda=0, n>0: logp=-inf, grad_lambda=inf (for one thing, because
log(1-1)=-inf and log(1-1+epsilon)>-inf)
lambda=inf, n<inf: logp=-inf, grad_lambda=-inf (because
log(gamma(lambda)) grows much faster than n*log(lambda))
lambda=inf, n=inf: domain error

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Poisson bounds checking
messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  We've got some limits to calc along with
a whole bunch of cdf gradients.

I didn't work through the actual limits before, but
my intuition was that poisson(n|lambda) would converge
to a delta function as n->0 and lambda->0.

0 log 0 is another case we might want to build
into our auto-diff.  There's no way to get this
out of basic log evaluation, though, because log(0) is
negative infinity and you evaluate compositionally.

Now if we had expression templates we might be able
to make it fly, but even then, it's a semantic not
a syntactic calc for the value of x in log(x) unless
the x is a structural 0 in a model somewhere.

- Bob

their own declarations.

- Bob

For a long time, I could build stan with g++ but not clang. This is
still the case now that I have clang 3.0. The error, after doing make
clean and make all, is eventually:

clang++ -O3 -Wall -g  -DNDEBUG  -I src -I lib -std=gnu++0x -I lib/
gtest/include  -I lib/gtest -DGTEST_HAS_PTHREAD=0 -lpthread src/test/
agrad/agrad_eigen_test.cpp lib/gtest/src/gtest_main.cc ar/libgtest.a -
o test/agrad/agrad_eigen
In file included from src/test/agrad/agrad_eigen_test.cpp:8:
In file included from src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp:6:
In file included from lib/Eigen/Dense:1:
In file included from lib/Eigen/Core:99:
In file included from /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/4.6/include/
emmintrin.h:36:
/usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/4.6/include/xmmintrin.h:102:19: error:
use of undeclared identifier '__builtin_ia32_addss'
  return (__m128) __builtin_ia32_addss ((__v4sf)__A, (__v4sf)__B);

Such errors are apparently due to a GCC-ism, see:

http://clang.llvm.org/compatibility.html#vector_builtins

which also includes a conversion script. But it is not clear whether
stan will still build with g++ if we convert so that stan will build
(for me) with clang. Also unclear is why stan builds for some of you
with Macs under either g++ or clang.

Ben

messages.subject: triangle distribution, bounds, NUTS hanging, and Pinocchioization
messages.subject_clean: triangle distribution, bounds, NUTS hanging, and Pinocchioization
messages.body_plain:
The triangle distro works out of the box.

src/demo/triangle.stan
-------------------------
parameters {
     double(-1.0,1.0) y;
}
model {
     lp__ <- lp__ + log(1.0 - abs(y));
}
------------------------

This model draws a single sample from the "unit"
triangle density with support on (-1,1) and density

p(y) = 1 - abs(y).

The parameter is declared with the bounds as a
constraint.  It uses the implicit variable "lp__"
to define the log probability function.  (This
maneuver will let us sum out discrete variables.)

With the bounds in place, here are the quantiles
from 3 runs:

     0%    25%    50%    75%   100%
-0.934 -0.318 -0.032  0.285  0.987

-0.983 -0.290 -0.026  0.315  0.971

-0.986 -0.303  0.003  0.283  0.931

The exact quantiles are (-1, -0.3, 0, 0.3, 1).

The density plot looks reasonably triangular too.

There seems to be an awful lot of rejection:

-0.123279
-0.24086
-0.24086
-0.24086
-0.24086
0.140527
0.140527
0.140527
-0.751579
-0.751579
-0.751579
-0.751579
0.87068
0.526088
0.746389
-0.636355
0.408008
0.408008
0.408008
0.408008

I'm wondering if this has anything to do with crossing
the undifferentiable point at zero.

Without the declared bounds on y, the current implementation
has problems.  It doesn't get into the corners and the 50%
intervals don't look good.

     0%    25%    50%    75%   100%
-0.805 -0.282  0.008  0.355  0.869

-0.892 -0.274 -0.017  0.267  0.856

-0.858 -0.273  0.007  0.338  0.885

-0.884 -0.315 -0.024  0.250  0.817

It can also hang during burn-in/adaptation (it hung
twice in 20 or so runs).  This is probably fixable.

I believe this is what one of Andrew's friends
hypothesized would happen (I'd be happy to cite
him or her in the doc).

There are also problems even with a bounded y if
I use the reflected triangle density, also with
support on (-1,1):

    p(y) = abs(y)

NUTS hangs in the burnin stage every time, even if
the initial value isn't zero.  I rather expected
it to shoot past the undifferentiable point at zero.

At a future Stan meeting, I can talk about some
Pinocchioization opportunities arising from Stan's
parameterization of the unbounded case (aka, more
fun with Jacobians).

- Bob

messages.subject: propto density summands & unit testing
messages.body_plain:
I'm in the middle of fixing multi normal and
noticed that there are not enough tests for propto.

You can drop a summand in a log probability if and
only if both

     1) propto == true, and
     2) there are no stan::agrad::var variables in the
        summand

Here's the first summand in the definition of multi_normal:

   if (!propto)
     lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI * y.rows()
           - 0.5 * log(Sigma.determinant());

This needs to be broken out into:

   if (!propto)
     lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI * y.rows();

   if (!propto || !is_constant<T_covar>::value)
     lp -=  0.5 * log(Sigma.determinant());

I'll add the is_constant<> metaprogramming for
vectors and matrices to support the static tests.

The other conditions need to be refined in the
same way.  If we include all the summands, we'll
get the right answer -- it'll only cost us some speed
and memory.  So feel free to leave things without
the propto calc -- we can optimize later in a way
that'll be backward compatible.

We will need tests for propto.  I think these should
be in the form of log difference tests, exploiting
the fact that we've tested foo<false> (full calc),
and that:

     foo<true>(theta1) - foo<true>(theta2)

     ==  foo<false>(theta1) - foo<false>(theta1)

So we can choose some pairs of theta1 and theta2,
then work through all the permutations of var
and constant testing the above.

This'll avoid the need to test exact values of
foo<true> (proportional calc), which may change over
time as we optimize.  (It won't if we minimize
the calcs the first time through.)

And the whole reason I dove into the class in the
first place is that we need to replace the direct calls
to Eigen's matrix ops with our own wrappers to take
care of promotion to auto-dif variables (alternatively,
we could promote within the probability calcs, but that
seems less modular).

- Bob

messages.subject: int_step function
messages.body_plain:
I think I forgot to send this a few days ago:

Stan is strongly typed, so you can't use a floating
point value where an integer is required, as in
array indexes or bounds for integer parameters or
vector dimensions.

To deal with the BUGS leuk and leukfr models,
I added a function to stan::maths:

     unsigned int int_step(double);

It's the integer return variant of
step(double), which returns a double.

I modified the BUGS examples leuk and leukfr
to use it.

I defined it in src/stan/maths/special_functions.hpp
and added a corresponding test set.

- Bob

>>> The other conditions need to be refined in the

>>> get the right answer -- it'll only cost us some speed
>>> and memory.  So feel free to leave things without
>>> the propto calc -- we can optimize later in a way
>>> that'll be backward compatible.
>>>

>>> be in the form of log difference tests, exploiting
>>> the fact that we've tested foo<false> (full calc),
>>> and that:
>>>
>>>    foo<true>(theta1) - foo<true>(theta2)
>>>
>>>    ==  foo<false>(theta1) - foo<false>(theta1)
>>>
>>> So we can choose some pairs of theta1 and theta2,
>>> then work through all the permutations of var
>>> and constant testing the above.
>>>
>>> This'll avoid the need to test exact values of
>>> foo<true> (proportional calc), which may change over
>>> time as we optimize.  (It won't if we minimize
>>> the calcs the first time through.)
>>>
>>> And the whole reason I dove into the class in the
>>> first place is that we need to replace the direct calls
>>> to Eigen's matrix ops with our own wrappers to take
>>> care of promotion to auto-dif variables (alternatively,
>>> we could promote within the probability calcs, but that
>>> seems less modular).
>>>
>>> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] propto density summands & unit testing
messages.body_plain:
I think it's OK to have unit tests depend on lower-level
functions that are themselves tested.  We don't need to
test compound functionality the pieces of which are unit
tested.  So just testing that we've defined the probability
densities so they can be auto-diffed is enough -- we don't
need to check the results (of course, it couldn't hurt and
redundant testing with different approaches is in general
a good thing).

There's nothing special about the y in y ~ Foo(theta),
You'll have to include it when it touches the params.
So it's usually still there following the same reules.

For instance, for log Beta(y|alpha,beta):

     summand                      include if variable
1)  - log B(alpha,beta)          alpha | beta
2)  + (alpha - 1) log(y)         alpha | y
3)  + (beta - 1) log(1 - y)      beta | y

Here (1) is a pure normalizing term only involving the
distribution arguments, but y touches the parameters
in terms (2) and (3).  The big savings is if alpha and
beta are constant, because (1) involves log gamma functions
and derivatives digamma functions as well.

- Bob

messages.subject: question about stan modeling language
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Bob.  I have some questions following up on our mtg last week.  The questions are, what happens under certain stan statements. I'm assuming there are four types of variables:  data, parameter, derived quantity, index.   I think I got some things wrong here so I'm setting it down so you can correct me.
A

1.  x ~ norm (mu, sigma)
If x is data, this adds a term to the log posterior
If x is a parameter, this adds a term to the log posterior
If x is a derived quantity, this returns an error?
If x is

2.  x <- y + z
If x is data, this does what?
If x is a parameter, this returns an error?
If x is a derived quantity, this tells stan to find all instances of "x" in the log posterior and replace it with "y + z". Also this tells stan to compute x as y+z and save it.
If x is an index, this returns an error?

3.  x <- norm (mu, sigma)
If x is data, this returns an error?
If x is a parameter, this returns an error?
If x is a derived quantity, this tells stan to draw from a normal, use it to compute x and save it.
If x is an index, this returns an error?

As you can see, one of the difficulties here is that derived quantities are being used in two ways, sometimes as intermediate steps in a calculation or in a specification of a distribution, sometimes as things to be saved in their own right.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] question about stan modeling language
messages.body_plain:
This is going to be a novel.  Are we meeting Wednesday?
We can discuss more.  I'm about to start writing the manual
as soon as I get the R interface done and it'll explain
all this from first principles.

1.  There are four flavors of declarations:

   constants: data & derived data
   variables: parameters & derived parameters

and two ways in which variables arise outside
of declarations:

    loop indexes (int)
    lp__ log probability value (double)

Data and derived data is "constant" in that it
acts like "data" in the R2Bugs sense and variables
are variable in that they act like "parameters"
in the R2Bugs sense.

Everything pretty much follows from the way each
statement type is translated.

    y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
    -------------------------------------------
    lp__ += normal_log(y,mu,sigma);

    y <- x + log(z);
    -------------------------------------------
    y = x + log(z);

    for (n in A:B) statement
    ------------------------------
    for (int n = A; n <= B; ++n) {
        statement'
    }

where statement' is the translation of the statement
making up the body of the for loop.

The initial value of lp__ is the sum of the log absolute
Jacobian determinants of all the variables declared with
transforms.  So if I declare

parameters{
     double(0,) tau;
}
-----------
lp__ += tau; // log transform

and tau gets transformed from the value provided by HMC or
NUTS using exp(tau_unbounded).

Further, integers are separated from doubles,
vectors, row vectors and matrices are included and
any of these can be put into arrays and declared
with various constraints like boundedness or
positive definiteness.

There isn't nearly as much error checking as
you may be expecting because the user can correct
things that may look like errors in other ways (e.g.,
by applying the Jacobian to a transform).  I'm mainly
checking well-formedness, existence of functions
and basic type compatibility.

For your case 1,

     y ~ norm(mu,sigma);

what happens depends on which eight patterns of
constant/variable we have.  Here's the actual code:

  ...
  normal_log(const T_y& y, const T_loc& mu, const T_scale& sigma,
  ...
       if (!propto
	  || !stan::is_constant<T_y>::value
	  || !stan::is_constant<T_loc>::value
	  || !stan::is_constant<T_scale>::value)
	lp -= square(y - mu) / (2.0 * square(sigma)); // SUMMAND 1
       if (!propto
	  || !stan::is_constant<T_scale>::value)
	lp -= log(sigma);                             // SUMMAND 2
       if (!propto)
	lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI;                    // SUMMAND 3

If we're not calculating proportionally, but fully, all three
summands get included.  If we're calculating proportionally,
we drop

     summand 3 always, because it's a constant normalizing term.

     summand 2 if sigma is constant

     summand 1 if all of y, mu and sigma are constant

Now keep in mind that any of y, mu or sigma can be a complex
expression involving other terms.  Any arithmetic operation
involving variables returns a variable; arithmetic ops with
all constant arguments return a constant.  So you can
literally write

     log(tau[n]) ~ normal(alpha * x[n] + beta, sigma);

if you want and exactly the same as the above will happen.

Now if you go and write such a thing and tau[n] is a parameter
(i.e., an auto-dif variable) rather than data (i.e., a double),
then you have to increment the log probability with the
log absolute derivative of the transform.

Here, the transform
is p(tau[n]) = p(log(tau[n])) | 1/tau[n] |

you'll have to also add the log of the absolute
value of the derivative, which in this case is:

     lp__ = lp__ - log(tau[n]);

Now you're good to go with parameter tau[n].  If we disallow
the first thing, we really cut down on the expressive power.
As is, you can just write out the whole density yourself by
increment lp__.  Doing that, you have plenty of rope to hang
yourself.

2.  x <- y + z just literally performs the assignment in
the order in which it is visited.  It's illegal only if
x is constant and y or z is variable.  Loop indexes are
treated just like any other variable, so if you write

     for (n in 1:N) {
         z[n] <- foo(x[n]);
         n <- n + 1;
     }

you'll only hit the odd numbers for n, assigning
z[1], z[3], z[5], ...

Variables and constants may be reassigned.  So you can
do this:

   for (n in 1:N) {
       mu <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
       y ~ normal(mu,1);
    }

Each trip through the loop, mu has a different value.
This is OK even if one or more of alpha, x[n] or beta
are variables.  This is a huge space savings on what
BUGS and JAGS require:

     mu[n] <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
     y ~ normal(mu[n],1);

You can still write it the BUGS way if you want.

If the left-hand-side is a parameter, it just gets
reassigned.  You lose the original connection to the
log probability as a parameter and it acts just like
a new derived value.  So you could save even more
space by finishing the calcuation with a parameter
that impacts the log probability, then reusing its storage.
(This won't save space, but I can see people trying it
and it'll do what they expect in acting like other local
parameter variables.)

3.  Right now, x <- norm(mu,sigma) is illegal because
norm isn't declared as a function.  I was thinking we could
add the random variate generators, at which point someone
could write:

    x <- rnorm(mu,sigma);

and it'd generate a random draw from norm(mu,sigma) and
assign it to x as described in 2.  The problem here is
that we don't want to auto-differentiate the random normal
generator, so I don't know how useful this will be as it'd
require either (a) mu and sigma to be constant data, or (b) it
to be "cut" in the BUGS sense so that the generation has no
bearing on the log probability function (this is what we
were talking about last time -- I'd thought before we could
do something more clever).

If Daniel's still reading at this point, we need overloaded
versions of rnorm that demote variables to constants, sort of
like we did the reverse for the matrix library for auto-dif.

Whew.

- Bob

On Dec 19, 2011, at 9:15 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> This is going to be a novel.  Are we meeting Wednesday?
> We can discuss more.  I'm about to start writing the manual
> as soon as I get the R interface done and it'll explain
> all this from first principles.
>
> 1.  There are four flavors of declarations:
>
>  constants: data & derived data
>  variables: parameters & derived parameters
>
> and two ways in which variables arise outside
> of declarations:
>
>   loop indexes (int)
>   lp__ log probability value (double)
>
> Data and derived data is "constant" in that it
> acts like "data" in the R2Bugs sense and variables
> are variable in that they act like "parameters"
> in the R2Bugs sense.
>
> Everything pretty much follows from the way each
> statement type is translated.
>
>   y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>   -------------------------------------------
>   lp__ += normal_log(y,mu,sigma);
>
>   y <- x + log(z);
>   -------------------------------------------
>   y = x + log(z);
>
>   for (n in A:B) statement
>   ------------------------------
>   for (int n = A; n <= B; ++n) {
>       statement'
>   }
>
> where statement' is the translation of the statement
> making up the body of the for loop.
>
> The initial value of lp__ is the sum of the log absolute
> Jacobian determinants of all the variables declared with
> transforms.  So if I declare
>
> parameters{
>    double(0,) tau;
> }
> -----------
> lp__ += tau; // log transform
>
> and tau gets transformed from the value provided by HMC or
> NUTS using exp(tau_unbounded).
>
> Further, integers are separated from doubles,
> vectors, row vectors and matrices are included and
> any of these can be put into arrays and declared
> with various constraints like boundedness or
> positive definiteness.
>
> There isn't nearly as much error checking as
> you may be expecting because the user can correct
> things that may look like errors in other ways (e.g.,
> by applying the Jacobian to a transform).  I'm mainly
> checking well-formedness, existence of functions
> and basic type compatibility.
>
> For your case 1,
>
>    y ~ norm(mu,sigma);
>
> what happens depends on which eight patterns of
> constant/variable we have.  Here's the actual code:
>
> ...
> normal_log(const T_y& y, const T_loc& mu, const T_scale& sigma,
> ...
>      if (!propto
> 	  || !stan::is_constant<T_y>::value
> 	  || !stan::is_constant<T_loc>::value
> 	  || !stan::is_constant<T_scale>::value)
> 	lp -= square(y - mu) / (2.0 * square(sigma)); // SUMMAND 1
>      if (!propto
> 	  || !stan::is_constant<T_scale>::value)
> 	lp -= log(sigma);                             // SUMMAND 2
>      if (!propto)
> 	lp += NEG_LOG_SQRT_TWO_PI;                    // SUMMAND 3
>
> If we're not calculating proportionally, but fully, all three
> summands get included.  If we're calculating proportionally,
> we drop
>
>    summand 3 always, because it's a constant normalizing term.
>
>    summand 2 if sigma is constant
>
>    summand 1 if all of y, mu and sigma are constant
>
> Now keep in mind that any of y, mu or sigma can be a complex
> expression involving other terms.  Any arithmetic operation
> involving variables returns a variable; arithmetic ops with
> all constant arguments return a constant.  So you can
> literally write
>
>    log(tau[n]) ~ normal(alpha * x[n] + beta, sigma);
>
> if you want and exactly the same as the above will happen.
>
> Now if you go and write such a thing and tau[n] is a parameter
> (i.e., an auto-dif variable) rather than data (i.e., a double),
> then you have to increment the log probability with the
> log absolute derivative of the transform.
>
> Here, the transform
> is p(tau[n]) = p(log(tau[n])) | 1/tau[n] |
>
> you'll have to also add the log of the absolute
> value of the derivative, which in this case is:
>
>    lp__ = lp__ - log(tau[n]);
>
> Now you're good to go with parameter tau[n].  If we disallow
> the first thing, we really cut down on the expressive power.
> As is, you can just write out the whole density yourself by
> increment lp__.  Doing that, you have plenty of rope to hang
> yourself.
>
> 2.  x <- y + z just literally performs the assignment in
> the order in which it is visited.  It's illegal only if
> x is constant and y or z is variable.  Loop indexes are
> treated just like any other variable, so if you write
>
>    for (n in 1:N) {
>        z[n] <- foo(x[n]);
>        n <- n + 1;
>    }
>
> you'll only hit the odd numbers for n, assigning
> z[1], z[3], z[5], ...
>
> Variables and constants may be reassigned.  So you can
> do this:
>
>  for (n in 1:N) {
>      mu <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
>      y ~ normal(mu,1);
>   }
>
> Each trip through the loop, mu has a different value.
> This is OK even if one or more of alpha, x[n] or beta
> are variables.  This is a huge space savings on what
> BUGS and JAGS require:
>
>    mu[n] <- alpha * x[n] + beta;
>    y ~ normal(mu[n],1);
>
> You can still write it the BUGS way if you want.
>
> If the left-hand-side is a parameter, it just gets
> reassigned.  You lose the original connection to the
> log probability as a parameter and it acts just like
> a new derived value.  So you could save even more
> space by finishing the calcuation with a parameter
> that impacts the log probability, then reusing its storage.
> (This won't save space, but I can see people trying it
> and it'll do what they expect in acting like other local
> parameter variables.)
>
> 3.  Right now, x <- norm(mu,sigma) is illegal because
> norm isn't declared as a function.  I was thinking we could
> add the random variate generators, at which point someone
> could write:
>
>   x <- rnorm(mu,sigma);

>
> Whew.
